nt: The pronoun **they** in this instance and in the rest of the verse likely refers to the Levites who were transporting the Box with accompanying music, as in [15:26](../15/26.md). It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [And the Levites brought in the Box of God]

The author assumes that readers will understand that by **they brought in the Box**, he means that the Levites brought the Box into the City of David, as he describes in [15:29](../15/29.md). You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [And the Levites brought the Box of God into the City of David]
Here, the **face** of God represents his “presence.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [in the presence of God]

x.ASV: And when David had made an end of offering the burnt-offering and the peace-offerings, he blessed the people in the name of Jehovah.
x.Darby: And when David had ended offering up the burnt-offerings and the peace-offerings, he blessed the people in the name of Jehovah.

nt: The author assumes that readers will understand that he is referring to a **burnt offering** and to **peace offerings** that David offered personally on this occasion. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [his own burnt offering and peace offerings]
To bless people **in the name of Yahweh** was to name Yahweh as the one whom one hoped and believed would bless those people. Alternate translation: [and he called upon Yahweh to bless the people]

x.ASV: And he dealt to every one of Israel, both man and woman, to every one a loaf of bread, and a portion of flesh, and a cake of raisins.
x.Darby: And he dealt to every one of Israel, both man and woman, to every one a loaf of bread and a measure [of wine] and a raisin-cake.

x.YLT: and giveth a portion to every man of Israel, both man and woman: to each a cake of bread, and a measure of wine, and a grape-cake.

nt: In each instance, the masculine term **man** has a generic sense that includes both men and women, as the context makes clear. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use language in your translation that is clearly inclusive of both men and women. Alternate translation: [to every person of Israel … to each person]
It might seem that including both of these expressions would be to express extra information in a way that would not be natural in your language. If so, you can omit the second expression.
The author is saying **every man of Israel** not to mean every single Israelite but those who were present. Alternate translation: [to every person who was present from throughout Israel]

x.ASV: And he appointed certain of the Levites to minister before the ark of Jehovah, and to celebrate and to thank and praise Jehovah, the God of Israel:
x.Darby: And he appointed certain of the Levites to do the service before the ark of Jehovah, and to celebrate, and to thank and praise Jehovah theGod of Israel:

x.YLT: And he putteth before the ark of Jehovah, of the Levites, ministers, even to make mention of, and to thank, and to give praise to Jehovah, God of Israel,

nt: Here, **to the face of** represents “in front of.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language, here and in verse 6. The UST models one way to do that.
וּ⁠לְ⁠הַזְכִּיר֙ וּ⁠לְ⁠הוֹד֣וֹת וּ⁠לְ⁠הַלֵּ֔ל לַ⁠יהוָ֖ה אֱלֹהֵ֥י יִשְׂרָאֵֽל

The author assumes that readers will understand that by **to make {one} remember**, he means that these Levites were to remind the Israelites, through their songs, of what Yahweh had done for them. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [to remind the Israelites what Yahweh, their God, had done for them and to thank and praise him for that]

nt: See how you translated the term “seconds” in [15:18](../15/18.md). Alternate translation: [his assistant]

x.ASV: and Benaiah and Jahaziel the priests with trumpets continually, before the ark of the covenant of God.
x.Darby: and Benaiah and Jahaziel the priests with trumpets continually, before the ark of the covenant ofGod.

x.YLT: and Benaiah and Jahaziel the priests are with trumpets continually before the ark of the covenant of God.

x.ASV: Then on that day did David first ordain to give thanks unto Jehovah, by the hand of Asaph and his brethren.
x.Darby: Then on that day David delivered first [this psalm] to give thanks to Jehovah through Asaph and his brethren.
x.KJV: Then on that day David delivered first this psalm to thank the Lord into the hand of Asaph and his brethren.
x.YLT: On that day then hath David given at the beginning to give thanks to Jehovah by the hand of Asaph and his brethren: --

nt: It might seem that saying both **On that day** and **then** would be to express extra information in a way that would not be natural in your language. If so, you can omit the term “then.” Alternate translation: [On that day David appointed]

The author assumes that readers will understand that by **that day**, he means the day when the Israelites brought the Box to Jerusalem. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [On the day when the Israelites brought the Box to Jerusalem,]

The author is using **at the first** as a common expression of his culture to mean “initially” or “for the first time.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [appointed for the first time] or [initially appointed]

Here, **hand** represents the agency of a person. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Asaph and his fellow Levites to be the ones to thank Yahweh]

In verses 8–36b, the author provides the words to a song that David apparently composed for this occasion and had Asaph and his fellow Levites sing. (Verse 36c tells how the Israelites responded afterwards.) In your translation, use a natural way of introducing this direct quotation of the words to this song. Alternate translation: [and his brothers, giving them this song to sing,]

x.ASV: O give thanks unto Jehovah, call upon his name; Make known his doings among the peoples.
x.Darby: Give thanks unto Jehovah, call upon his name; Make known his acts among the peoples.
x.KJV: Give thanks unto the Lord, call upon his name, make known his deeds among the people.
x.YLT: Give thanks to Jehovah, call in His name, Make known among the peoples His doings.

nt: See the discussion in the introduction to this chapter of how portions of this song constitute all or part of several psalms in the book of Psalms. If you have already translated those psalms, that will help you translate this song. See the chapter introduction for a list of what psalm passages correspond to which portions.

The implied “you” in the imperatives **Give thanks**, **call**, and **make known** is plural because David, through this song, is addressing all the Israelites who are present. So use the plural form in your translation if your language marks that distinction. The imperatives in the rest of the song are also plural.

David is using **call on his name** as a common expression of the culture to mean “acknowledge him as your God.” He means that the Israelites whom he is addressing should acknowledge Yahweh by name as their God. If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [acknowledge him as your God]

x.ASV: Sing unto him, sing praises unto him; Talk ye of all his marvellous works.
x.Darby: Sing unto him, sing psalms unto him; Meditate upon all his wondrous works.
x.KJV: Sing unto him, sing psalms unto him, talk ye of all his wondrous works.
x.YLT: Sing ye to Him, sing psalms to Him, Meditate on all His wonders.

x.ASV: Glory ye in his holy name; Let the heart of them rejoice that seek Jehovah.
x.Darby: Glory in his holy name: Let the heart of them rejoice that seek Jehovah.
x.KJV: Glory ye in his holy name: let the heart of them rejoice that seek the Lord.
x.YLT: Boast yourselves in His holy name, Rejoice doth the heart of those seeking Jehovah.

nt: David is using the possessive form to describe a **name** that is characterized by **holiness**. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [in his holy name]

Here, Yahweh’s **name** represents Yahweh himself, who is holy. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [in Yahweh, who is holy]

David is using one part of a person, his **heart** (representing the location of his desires), to mean all of him in the act of rejoicing. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [let the people who seek Yahweh rejoice]

David is speaking of these people as if they were looking for Yahweh, as if he were a lost object. In this context, to seek Yahweh means generally to choose to know, worship, and obey him. Alternate translation: [those who worship Yahweh] or [those who are loyal to Yahweh]

x.ASV: Seek ye Jehovah and his strength; Seek his face evermore.
x.Darby: Seek Jehovah and his strength, Seek his face continually;
x.KJV: Seek the Lord and his strength, seek his face continually.
x.YLT: Seek ye Jehovah and His strength, Seek His face continually.

nt: The name **Yahweh** and the term **strength** together express a single idea. David is referring to **strength** that **Yahweh** provides. If it would be more natural in your language, you could express this meaning in a different way. Alternate translation: [Seek strength from Yahweh]

David is continuing to speak as if people should look for Yahweh. In this context, to **Seek** Yahweh means to depend on him. Alternate translation: [Depend on Yahweh for strength] or [Pray to Yahweh for strength]
Here, Yahweh’s **face** represents his presence. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [search for his presence]

David is continuing to speak as if people should look for Yahweh. In this context, to **search** for Yahweh’s presence means to endeavor to be in it. Alternate translation: [endeavor to be in his presence]

x.ASV: Remember his marvellous works that he hath done, His wonders, and the judgments of his mouth,
x.Darby: Remember his wondrous works which he hath done; His miracles, and the judgments of his mouth:
x.KJV: Remember his marvellous works that he hath done, his wonders, and the judgments of his mouth;
x.YLT: Remember His wonders that He did, His signs, and the judgments of His mouth,

nt: Here Yahweh’s **mouth** represents what he has said. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and the judgments that he has spoken]

x.ASV: O ye seed of Israel his servant, Ye children of Jacob, his chosen ones.
x.Darby: Ye seed of Israel his servant, Ye sons of Jacob, his chosen ones.
x.KJV: O ye seed of Israel his servant, ye children of Jacob, his chosen ones.
x.YLT: O seed of Israel, His servant, O sons of Jacob, His chosen ones!

nt: David is using the term **seed** to mean “descendants.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [descendants of Israel]
The pronoun **his** refers to Yahweh. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [Yahweh’s servant]

David is speaking as if the people of Israel were the **sons** of Jacob. He means that they are his descendants. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [descendants of Jacob]
While the term **chosen** is a noun, it may be natural in some languages to specify an agent, as if this were a passive verbal form. Alternate translation: [whom he has chosen]

x.ASV: He is Jehovah our God; His judgments are in all the earth.
x.Darby: He, Jehovah, is ourGod; His judgments are in all the earth.
x.KJV: He is the Lord our God; his judgments are in all the earth.
x.YLT: He is Jehovah our God, In all the earth are His judgments.

nt: By using the possessive form **our God**, David is not saying that the Israelites possess or control Yahweh. Rather, he is using these words to indicate that Yahweh is the God whom the Israelites worship. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. The UST models one way to do that.

When David says that Yahweh’s judgments are **in** all of the earth, he means that they apply to all people everywhere on the earth. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [his laws apply to everyone on earth]

x.ASV: Remember his covenant for ever, The word which he commanded to a thousand generations,
x.Darby: Be ye ever mindful of his covenant, The word which he commanded to a thousand generations, —
x.KJV: Be ye mindful always of his covenant; the word which he commanded to a thousand generations;
x.YLT: Remember ye to the age His covenant, The word He commanded--To a thousand generations,

nt: זִכְר֤וּ לְ⁠עוֹלָם֙ בְּרִית֔⁠וֹ דָּבָ֥ר צִוָּ֖ה לְ⁠אֶ֥לֶף דּֽוֹר

These two phrases mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. You could combine the phrases and express the emphasis in another way. However, since Hebrew poetry was based on this kind of repetition, you may want to show this to your readers by including both phrases in your translation. If it would be helpful, you could connect the phrases in a way that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. Decide as a team how you will approach pairs of phrases that mean basically the same thing. (You may already have done this if you have previously translated poetical or prophetic books.) Alternate translation: [Remember his covenant forever, yes, remember the word he commanded for a thousand generations]

In this context, the term **Remember** means to do more than recall information about something. David is using the term to mean “obey.” You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [Obey the terms of his covenant]

David is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [remember for a thousand generations the word he commanded ]

David is using the term **word** to represent what Yahweh said by using words. If it would be clearer in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the decree that he spoke]
David is saying **a thousand** as an overstatement for emphasis. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a different way to express the emphasis. The UST models one way to do that.

x.ASV: The covenant which he made with Abraham, And his oath unto Isaac,
x.Darby: Which he made with Abraham, And of his oath unto Isaac;
x.KJV: Even of the covenant which he made with Abraham, and of his oath unto Isaac;
x.YLT: Which He hath made with Abraham, And His oath--to Isaac,

nt: See how you translated the term “cut” in [11:3](../11/03.md). Alternate translation: [he made]

David does not mean that the Israelites should remember two things, Yahweh’s “covenant” (verse 15) and this **oath**. David is speaking of this oath to represent that same covenant, which Yahweh confirmed to Isaac with an oath. Alternate translation: [and which he confirmed by an oath to Isaac]

x.ASV: And confirmed the same unto Jacob for a statute, To Israel for an everlasting covenant,
x.Darby: And he confirmed it unto Jacob for a statute, Unto Israel for an everlasting covenant,
x.KJV: And hath confirmed the same to Jacob for a law, and to Israel for an everlasting covenant,
x.YLT: And He establisheth it to Jacob for a statute, To Israel--a covenant age-during.

nt: וַ⁠יַּעֲמִידֶ֤⁠הָ לְ⁠יַעֲקֹב֙ לְ⁠חֹ֔ק לְ⁠יִשְׂרָאֵ֖ל בְּרִ֥ית עוֹלָֽם

Recall how you have decided to translate poetic pairs of statements that mean basically the same thing. Alternate translation: [And he confirmed it to Jacob as a statute, indeed, he confirmed it to Israel as a covenant forever]
The pronoun **it** refers back to verse 15 to Yahweh’s covenant. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [and he confirmed his covenant to Jacob as a statute]

In this context, the term **statute** does not refer to a law that the Israelites needed to keep. It describes a decree that Yahweh made that he would definitely carry out. Alternate translation: [as something that he would certainly do]

The author is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [he confirmed it to Israel as a covenant forever]

**Israel** and **Jacob** are two names for the same individual. So that readers do not misunderstand and think that “Israel” means the nation here, it may be helpful to use a pronoun that refers back to Jacob. Alternate translation: [to him]

x.ASV: Saying, Unto thee will I give the land of Canaan, The lot of your inheritance;
x.Darby: Saying, Unto thee will I give the land of Canaan, The lot of your inheritance;
x.KJV: Saying, Unto thee will I give the land of Canaan, the lot of your inheritance;
x.YLT: Saying: To thee I give the land of Canaan, The portion of your inheritance,

nt: לֵ⁠אמֹ֗ר לְ⁠ךָ֙ אֶתֵּ֣ן אֶֽרֶץ־כְּנָ֔עַן חֶ֖בֶל נַחֲלַתְ⁠כֶֽם

If it would be clearer in your language, you could translate this so that there is not a quotation within a quotation. Alternate translation: [telling him that he would give him the land of Canaan as the portion of his inheritance]

The word **you** is plural because Yahweh was addressing Jacob individually. The word **your** is plural because Yahweh was referring to Jacob and his descendants. Use the appropriate singular and plural forms in your translation if your language marks that distinction.

Yahweh was speaking of the **land of Canaan** as if it were something that Jacob would inherit as his share of property from a relative who had died. He was doing that to represent the land as something that would always belong to Jacob and his descendants. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. The UST models one way to do that.

x.ASV: When ye were but a few men in number, Yea, very few, and sojourners in it;
x.Darby: When ye were a few men in number, Of small account, and strangers in it.
x.KJV: When ye were but few, even a few, and strangers in it.
x.YLT: When ye are few of number, As a little thing, and sojourners in it.

nt: David is speaking as if the Israelites he is addressing through this song had actually been present at this time and been **few in number**. He is addressing them as representatives of their nation. Alternate translation: [when the people of your nation were] or [when your ancestors were]

David is using **according to a little** as a common expression of his culture to mean “very small.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [a tiny group] or [quite small]

The phrases **few in number** and **according to a little** mean basically the same thing. David is using the two phrases together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [only a small group of people]
The pronoun **it** refers back to “the land of Canaan” in the previous verse. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [in that land]

x.ASV: And they went about from nation to nation, And from one kingdom to another people.
x.Darby: And they went from nation to nation, And from one kingdom to another people.
x.KJV: And when they went from nation to nation, and from one kingdom to another people;
x.YLT: And they go up and down, From nation unto nation, And from a kingdom unto another people.

nt: David is still speaking of the ancestors of the Israelites, but he is now doing so in the third person. (People writing poetry in Hebrew often shifted between persons in this way.) If it would be helpful to your readers, you could clarify how David is making this transition. Alternate translation: [And your ancestors wandered]

x.ASV: He suffered no man to do them wrong; Yea, he reproved kings for their sakes,
x.Darby: He suffered no man to oppress them, And reproved kings for their sakes,
x.KJV: He suffered no man to do them wrong: yea, he reproved kings for their sakes,
x.YLT: He hath not suffered any to oppress them, And reproveth on their account kings:

nt: In this context, **a man** means **anyone**. Alternate translation: [anyone]

x.ASV: Saying, Touch not mine anointed ones, And do my prophets no harm.
x.Darby: [Saying,] Touch not mine anointed ones, And do my prophets no harm.
x.KJV: Saying, Touch not mine anointed, and do my prophets no harm.
x.YLT: Come not against Mine anointed ones, And against My prophets do not evil.

nt: This is a direct quotation of Yahweh. In your translation, use a natural way of introducing direct quotations in your language. Alternate translation: [saying, ‘May you not touch my anointed {ones}, and may you not harm my prophets’]

If it would be clearer in your language, you could translate this so that there is not a quotation within a quotation. Alternate translation: [telling them not to touch his anointed and not harm to his prophets]

While Yahweh is using a verbal form that communicates what someone wishes another person would do, this is actually a strong command. If it would be clearer in your language, you could use a command form in your translation. The UST models one way to do that.
In this context, the term **touch** as the same meaning as **harm** in the next line. Alternate translation: [May you not harm] or [Do not harm]

The expression **anointed** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that would be natural in your language. Alternate translation: [the ones whom I have anointed]

Yahweh is speaking as if he had actually **anointed** all of the Israelites. He means that he has chosen them and set them apart for the special task of being his people, just as a person in this culture would be anointed when assuming an important position such as king or high priest. Alternate translation: [my chosen ones] or [the ones whom I have chosen]

x.ASV: Sing unto Jehovah, all the earth; Show forth his salvation from day to day.
x.Darby: Sing unto Jehovah, all the earth; Publish his salvation from day to day.
x.KJV: Sing unto the Lord, all the earth; shew forth from day to day his salvation.
x.YLT: Sing to Jehovah, all the earth, Proclaim from day unto day His salvation.

nt: Here, **all of the earth** represents all the people who live on the earth. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [all you people who live on the earth]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **salvation**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [that he is the one who saves]

David is using **from day to day** as a common expression of his culture to mean “every day” or “continually.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [every day] or [continually]

x.ASV: Declare his glory among the nations, His marvellous works among all the peoples.
x.Darby: Declare his glory among the nations, His wondrous works among all peoples.
x.KJV: Declare his glory among the heathen; his marvellous works among all nations.
x.YLT: Rehearse among nations His glory, Among all the peoples His wonders.

nt: If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **glory**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [that he is glorious]

The author is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [recount his wonderful doings among all of the peoples]

x.ASV: For great is Jehovah, and greatly to be praised: He also is to be feared above all gods.
x.Darby: For Jehovah is great, and exceedingly to be praised; And he is terrible above allgods.
x.KJV: For great is the Lord, and greatly to be praised: he also is to be feared above all gods.
x.YLT: For great is Jehovah, and praised greatly, And fearful He is above all gods.

nt: The word translated as **For** indicates that what follows is a reason for what came before. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that what follows is a reason for what came before. Alternate translation: [Do this because]

The expression **is {to be} praised** is a passive verbal form. If your language would not use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [and everyone should praise him]

The expression **is {to be} feared** is a passive verbal form. If your language would not use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [and everyone should fear him]

x.ASV: For all the gods of the peoples are idols: But Jehovah made the heavens.
x.Darby: For all thegods of the peoples are idols; But Jehovah made the heavens.
x.KJV: For all the gods of the people are idols: but the Lord made the heavens.
x.YLT: For all gods of the peoples are nought, And Jehovah the heavens hath made.

nt: Here the word **For** introduces not a reason but an explanation. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a different connecting word to show how this statement relates to what comes before it. Alternate translation: [After all,]

x.Darby: Majesty and splendour are before him; Strength and gladness in his place.

nt: Here, Yahweh’s **face** represents his “presence”. Alternate translation: [Splendor and majesty are in his presence]
